title: Nihang speech
hook: Nihangs speak in bold, playful coded phrases, like calling one Sikh a hundred and twenty-five thousand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nihang dals: the nagara in front, and Kabir's hero who never leaves the field. Your line was the blue army. Who did you stand up for? Day one thousand three hundred nine.

A lone rider comes into a village and someone asks how many are with him. He grins and says: a whole army. He's alone. He isn't lying, not by his own way of speaking. Families do a small version of this. A dented old car gets called the limo. A sandwich at midnight is the feast. A kid who's scared of the dark is the brave one. The names aren't mistakes. They're a way of standing up straight. This week we met the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers and the riders. We close the week with the riders' language.
screen: `A LONE RIDER: A WHOLE ARMY.` → `THE DENTED CAR IS THE LIMO.` → `NAMES THAT STAND UP STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Nihangs have their own way of talking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's speech. It's full of bold, playful names for ordinary things. Tradition says it grew up in the hard years, among riders who had very little, and it turned want into plenty with a word. A plain meal can get a grand name. Danger gets a joke for a name. One well-worn example is the one in today's hook. A single Nihang may call himself sava lakh. Lakh means a hundred thousand; sava means one and a quarter. So: one Sikh is a hundred and twenty-five thousand. That phrase comes from a saying that tradition puts in Guru Gobind Singh's mouth, in paraphrase: I will make sparrows strike down hawks, and set one to fight a hundred and twenty-five thousand. Only then will I be called Gobind Singh. Here's what the speech is doing. It isn't a boast about strength. It's a refusal to feel small. If you're one, and there are many against you, the speech says: one is enough. Now, the Guru Granth Sahib keeps that boldness in balance. In a salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is frightened of no one, call that one wise. Read the two together. The bold name is for not being afraid. It's never for making someone else afraid. A Nihang calling himself an army is standing up straight, not standing over anyone. And notice the play in it. Nihang speech is funny on purpose. Courage with a smile on it is harder to crush.
screen: `KHALSA BOLE: THE RIDERS' SPEECH.` · `SAVA LAKH: ONE AS AN ARMY.` · `FEAR NO ONE, FRIGHTEN NO ONE.` · `COURAGE WITH A SMILE ON IT.` · then, large: `ONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say something boldly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place in your life where you feel outnumbered: a meeting, a family argument, a task too big for one person. Now give yourself a bold name for it, a little playful, the way a rider would. Not to frighten anyone; just to stand up straight. Say it silently on the out-breath. Then let the salok in, one half on each breath. In: frighten no one. Out: fear no one. The bell holds the time.
Nihang speech. The Khalsa's bold, playful names, like sava lakh, one rider counted as a hundred and twenty-five thousand. Today's word.
Your line: one is enough. Today, when you feel outnumbered, use your bold name once, out loud or in your head, and then do the next thing anyway. Day one thousand three hundred nine.
